title: Cavity-assisted homodyne detection with a single photodiode
abstract: High-frequency squeezed states are important for quantum metrology and information processing, but quadrature measurements at gigahertz frequencies remain challenging. Balanced homodyne detection (BHD), the standard approach, requires closely matched complex transfer functions in both photodetection channels to suppress local-oscillator (LO) noise and maintain a well-defined readout quadrature. This matching becomes increasingly difficult at high bandwidths. Strongly asymmetric single-photodiode homodyne detection avoids this requirement, but achieving high signal efficiency and shot-noise clearance typically requires hundreds of milliwatts of LO power and does not suppress technical LO sidebands. I propose cavity-assisted homodyne detection, in which the quantum field and LO enter separate ports of an impedance-matched traveling-wave cavity. The resonant LO carrier is transmitted to the photodetector, where it beats with off-resonant signal sidebands reflected from the cavity. At the same time, technical LO sidebands outside the cavity linewidth are suppressed. I derive the quantum input-output relations and linearized photocurrent including intracavity loss, and show that near-unity signal-transfer efficiency can be achieved at moderate incident LO power. The cavity linewidth and free spectral range determine the usable detection band.
summary: This paper introduces cavity-assisted homodyne detection as an advanced technique for measuring quantum quadratures at high frequencies. By coupling the signal and local oscillator through a resonant cavity, it overcomes the need for perfectly matched photodetection channels required by standard methods. The resulting setup offers high signal efficiency and superior suppression of technical noise sidebands using only a single photodiode.
main_problem: Measuring quadrature components of high-frequency squeezed states is challenging, especially at gigahertz frequencies, due to limitations in standard detection methods.
main_result: Cavity-assisted homodyne detection achieves near-unity signal-transfer efficiency at moderate LO power while effectively suppressing technical LO noise sidebands.
method: The authors derive quantum input-output relations for a traveling-wave cavity where the signal and LO interact, leading to a single-photodiode readout.
model_or_system: The system uses an impedance-matched traveling-wave ring cavity where the quantum signal enters one port and the LO enters a separate port. The detection relies on the LO carrier beating with off-resonant signal sidebands reflected from the cavity.
key_observables: The photocurrent $\delta \hat{I}(\Omega)$ and the signal-transfer efficiency $\eta_{	ext{cav}}(\Omega)$.
important_parameters: Cavity linewidth ($\kappa$), Free Spectral Range (FSR), and the ratio of LO power to signal power.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the detected LO carrier amplitude dominates the residual signal carrier amplitude, and the cavity is impedance-matched.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the concept of signal and LO entering separate ports of the cavity, resulting in the detected field. Figure 2 shows the partitioning of the unit transfer coefficients ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$, $|t|^2$, $|l|^2$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of BHD, then proposes the cavity-assisted setup, deriving the input-output relations. Subsequent sections analyze the noise suppression and compare the single-photodiode readout against alternative methods like beam-splitter readouts.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for implementing high-bandwidth quantum measurements using cavity QED principles, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems and quantum optics.
